https://www.dw.com/en/albania-as-corrupt.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NSZ5 Vlora Hyseni, former head of Albania's State Intelligence Service, leaves the offices of Albania's Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organized Crime (SPAK), where she answered questions about her alleged involvement in a major corruption scandal Image: Armando Babani/Matrix Images/picture alliance Advertisement On September 22, the head of Albania 's State Intelligence Service, Vlora Hyseni, was in Baku, Azerbaijan, attending an international conference of intelligence service chiefs. Back in Tirana, the Special Court had ordered her house arrest over two suspected criminal offences: supporting the perpetrator of a crime and disclosure of investigative secrecy. The investigation into Hyseni emerged from a wider corruption case involving the National Agency for Information Society (AKSHI), the agency responsible for much of Albania's digital public infrastructure. Prosecutors suspect that she used information available to her as intelligence chief to help a person wanted in that investigation. Hyseni turned herself in to the Albanian authorities later that day and remains under house arrest as the investigation continues. She has since been dismissed as head of the intelligence service. Rise in criminal proceedings and investigations Hyseni's case is the latest in a series of criminal proceedings that have reached unusually high into Albania's political and state establishment. Political scientist Afrim Krasniqi says that after the 2016 reform, Albania's new justice institutions were expected to 'focus on high-level corruption and "VIP" cases' Image: Afrim Krasniqi/Privatarchiv A former president has spent almost two years in detention, a former prime minister is on trial, the mayor of Tirana has been behind bars since early 2025, two former deputy prime ministers under Prime Minister Edi Rama have also faced criminal proceedings, and investigations have been launched into senior officials in agencies controlling large areas of public spending and state infrastructure. These are all separate cases, but they all involve alleged abuse of public power. How did Albania get here? For years, the problem was completely the opposite: High-level corruption in Albania was widely associated with impunity . This is why bringing senior political figures accused of wrongdoing before the courts became one of the central expectations of the justice reform launched in 2016 . "The expectation was that the new justice institutions would focus on high-level corruption and 'VIP' cases," says Afrim Krasniqi, a political scientist and executive director of the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. "There were individuals who stood above the law, and impunity was pronounced," he told DW. Dorian Matlija says that Albania is 'becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it' Image: Kristi Çavo The reform fundamentally reshaped Albania's justice system and created new institutions to investigate corruption and organized crime, including the Special Anti-Corruption Structure, SPAK. But the change was not immediate. Building the new institutions took years, and older cases were often more difficult to investigate. For Dorian Matlija, a lawyer and executive director of Albanian civil society organization Res Publica, the number of senior officials now facing criminal proceedings does not necessarily mean that corruption is more widespread today than it was in the past. "What has changed significantly is the institutional reaction," Matlija told DW. "Today, SPAK is a specialized structure with greater independence, stronger capacities and international support, as well as the willingness to undertake investigations that have broken the myth of the untouchability of senior officials." The other side of accountability But bringing senior officials before the courts is only one measure of whether institutions are working. Albania applied for EU membership in 2009 and was granted candidate status in June 2014. Pictured here: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen (both center) Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS By the time a corruption case reaches prosecutors, the alleged abuse has already taken place. For Matlija, this is where Albania's progress is far less clear. "We are becoming more effective at punishing corruption after it has occurred, but much less capable of preventing it," he said. Matlija points to the institutions and mechanisms that are supposed to act before a case becomes criminal: administrative controls, audits, conflict-of-interest rules and asset declarations. In his assessment, these have often proved ineffective. The European Commission's 2025 report on Albania reaches a similar conclusion. It said that SPAK has made "tangible progress towards a solid track record in the fight against corruption." At the same time, the report says that corruption remains widespread and that "the institutional framework for prevention of corruption continued to have a limited impact." The impact on citizens The problem is also visible in citizens' encounters with public officials. In a 2023 survey by the anti-corruption and good governance coalition SELDI (Southeast Europe Leadership for Development and Integrity) , 52% of respondents in Albania said they had experienced corruption pressure from public officials, while 40% reported having paid a bribe. Krasniqi sees the problem in broader political terms. Albania has been governed by Rama's Socialist Party since 2013, and the party currently holds an outright majority in parliament. He argues that this prolonged political dominance has weakened the checks and balances that should constrain the executive. "We have a deformed system," he said. "The head of the executive controls the executive, parliament and institutions." He argues that this concentration of power has been accompanied by informal networks of influence, with people outside state institutions able to shape political decisions, legislation and the use of public assets. Rama has repeatedly maintained that criminal responsibility is individual when investigations have reached senior officials. Responding to the Hyseni case, he returned to the same position. "When a senior official has opened an account with justice, the case of the former intelligence chief is an individual matter between her and the justice system," Rama said. What does this mean for Albania's EU accession hopes? In May, the EU confirmed that the country had met the interim benchmarks for the "fundamentals" cluster, which includes the rule of law, and moved into a phase focused on implementation and lasting results. Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index shows Albania improving from 33 points in 2012 to 39 in 2025 but still ranking below all EU member states. For Matlija, Albania's efforts to advance EU integration helped create the conditions that allowed institutions such as SPAK to become stronger and more independent. "The EU no longer demands only the adoption of laws and reforms, but also concrete and sustainable results. This creates constant pressure for justice institutions to be genuinely effective and independent of political power," he said. For Krasniqi, this is also where the meaning of European integration lies. Membership, he argues, should not be judged only by Albania's progress through the formal accession process, but by whether the country itself changes. "The essence should be for Albania, Albanian society and Albanian institutions to change and improve, so that we become worthy of integration," he said. For him, that change should also be felt by citizens through greater social security, prosperity and independence, rather than being just a series of formal achievements. The handover comes after an agreement between the countries, in which Bulgaria would return relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war. Photograph: Lambros Kazanas/Alamy Bulgaria Remains of medieval tsar return to Bulgaria after decades-long dispute with Greece Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel will help persuade Britain to return Parthenon marbles Associated Press in Thessaloniki Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.31 EDT Last modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 06.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel will arrive in Bulgaria on Saturday amid great pomp and ceremony, after decades of negotiations with neighbouring Greece. Greek PM: deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached with ‘political will and courage’ Read more The remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are to be flown to the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, onboard a military aircraft to be received with full state honours, including a fighter jet escort, a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects. The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, said he hoped the handover would bolster Athens’s campaign to persuade Britain to return the Parthenon marbles , a collection of 2,500-year-old sculptures taken from the Acropolis and held by the British Museum. “The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he said. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.” View image in fullscreen Bulgaria’s military personnel carry a coffin with the remains of medieval ruler Tsar Samuel during a handover ceremony in Thessaloniki. Photograph: Giannis Papanikos/AP Samuel was a warrior ruler who battled the Byzantine empire to expand his kingdom, but was ultimately defeated and died shortly afterwards in 1014. He is considered a symbol of Bulgaria’s national identity. The handover of his remains follows an agreement earlier this week between the two countries’ culture ministers, under which Bulgaria will return religious relics taken from Greek monasteries during the first world war. Several prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have raised concerns about the adequacy of Bulgaria’s contributions. Mitsotakis and his Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, attended a ceremony at Thessaloniki’s Museum of Byzantine Civilization, where the remains were kept, before the handover. “These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors,” Radev said, speaking at the ceremony held at the museum. “If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger,” Radev said. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: 1:38 Beau Lamarre-Condon at McDonald's drive-thru in van used to allegedly dispose of bodies – video New South Wales Beau Lamarre-Condon visits McDonald’s drive-thru in van allegedly used to dispose of bodies, in CCTV shown to jury CCTV footage shows the police officer buying fast food, attending hospital, and visiting three separate Bunnings stores in the days after the alleged murder Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.07 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 03.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Beau Lamarre-Condon ordered food from a McDonald’s drive-thru in a van allegedly used to dispose of two bodies, footage released by the court has shown. Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple, Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. Exhibits newly released by the court showed the officer’s movements in the days after the alleged double murder. During the early hours of 22 February 2024, Lamarre-Condon is captured by the cameras at McDonald’s Sutton Forest, about 30km from where he would allegedly dispose of Baird and Davies’ bodies. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In the video, he pulls up to the drive-thru in a white van, pays for his order, then moves to the next window where he collects a paper McDonald’s bag and a drink. It’s the latest footage seen by the jury in Lamarre-Condon’s murder trial, which has been running for five weeks. Last week, CCTV showing his movements the day after the alleged shootings was played in the NSW supreme court. He can be seen near Baird’s house carrying a bucket, withdrawing cash from various ATMs, and buying cleaning items from Bunnings Alexandria. Beau Lamarre-Condon goes to St Vincent's Hospital to undergo minor surgery – video Footage from Cronulla on the evening of 20 February 2024 shows Lamarre-Condon and a friend dining at a sushi train before taking a walk along the esplanade at the beach. Later that night, the pair stop by Cronulla Bowls Club and the friend points out the skip bins, before Lamarre-Condon returns alone a few hours afterwards. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly played Taylor Swift’s No Body, No Crime during body disposal, court told Read more Bloodied items belonging to Baird and Davies would be found inside the bins the next morning. Videos from two days after the alleged murders were also played to the jury on Monday, and released late Wednesday. About 7.30am on 21 February 2024, footage from St Vincent’s hospital in Sydney showed Lamarre-Condon arriving for a minor surgery, the day after he allegedly cleaned up the scene of the crime. Beau Lamarre-Condon picks up items at Bunnings Rockdale – video In CCTV from Bunnings Rockdale, Lamarre-Condon can be seen pushing a shopping trolley through the aisles before eventually buying gloves, a shovel, a wheelbarrow, and quick-set concrete, among other items. Later that afternoon, footage from Bunnings Goulburn – about 150km away – captures the policeman and his friend speaking to a sales assistant and buying an angle grinder and padlock. Baird and Davies’ bodies would be discovered in nearby Bungonia a few days later. The defence team claims the two men were accidentally shot when the accused acted in “self-defence”. Lamarre-Condon then “panicked considerably”, cleaning up the scene and disposing of the bodies, defence lawyer John Stratton SC said. The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
